title: The Mill and the Flat Lid: Anchay, the Empress's Packer, and the Workshop by the River
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Anchay, birth at the mill of Charbouilla
stops.date_confidence: attested; day and year given by both Wikipedia editions and Wikidata Q277616. The hamlet of Anchay lies in the commune of Lavans-sur-Valouse, merged into Saint-Hymetiere-sur-Valouse on 1 January 2019; the coordinate is the commune centre, since the mill itself is not separately mapped. The first pass's population figure of 148 was the 1999 census and is dropped.
stops.campa: The Vuitton are millers, carpenters, and farmers in the hills above the Valouse, and at the water mill of Charbouilla, in the hamlet of Anchay, a son is born on the fourth of August. The commune is Lavans-sur-Valouse. It will keep that name until 2019, when it is folded into Saint-Hymetiere-sur-Valouse and goes off the map. The child is called Louis. His mother makes hats; his father works wood and water. He is expected to take the mill in his turn, as the family has done.
suggested_refs: The water mill of Charbouilla at Anchay, and the civil registers of Lavans-sur-Valouse, never opened in this research

stops.name: Anchay, the mother dies
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; only 'about ten years old' is given, by en.wikipedia alone. The mother's name, the day, and the cause are in no source consulted. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Louis is about ten when his mother dies. She was a hat-maker. The father remarries, and the surviving accounts describe a stepmother the boy does not get on with. He stays at the mill, set to the family trade of water and grain and the turning stone, which is what his father wants of him. No register consulted in this pass gives the woman's name or the day of her death. The whole episode rests on a single encyclopedia summary and not on any document at all.
suggested_refs: The Jura civil registers for Lavans-sur-Valouse, 1825-1835, unconsulted

stops.name: Anchay, the boy walks out
stops.date_confidence: year attested; en.wikipedia gives spring 1835 at age 13, Encyclopedia.com gave 14. The contradiction is carried, not resolved. Month set to March for 'spring'; the day is a default.
stops.campa: In the spring he walks out of Anchay and turns north, thirteen years old by one account and fourteen by another, against his father's wish that he stay at the mill. The distance ahead of him is given as four hundred kilometres by the French sources and as two hundred and ninety-two miles by the English, which is four hundred and seventy. The two figures stand seventy kilometres apart and no source reconciles them. He carries nothing and has no trade. He will take work for food and lodging as he goes, and the walk will last two years.
suggested_refs: The two irreconcilable distances, 400 km in French and 292 miles in English, printed side by side

stops.name: Between the Jura and the Ile-de-France, no town named
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the coordinate is a marker rather than a stage: no source consulted names a single village, town, or river crossing on this route, so the pin is set at the midpoint of the straight line from Anchay to Paris. Date defaulted to the middle year of the two-year walk.
stops.campa: For two years he is on the road between the Jura and the Ile-de-France, working as he goes: stable work, kitchen work, whatever a boy without papers can find between one town and the next. Not one source consulted names a single village on this route. The country he crossed and the winters he spent in it are absent from every account of him, and so is whatever trade he touched before he found his own. The walk is the founding scene of the house's telling of itself. It is also the least documented thing in his life.
suggested_refs: The undocumented route from the Jura to Paris, 1835-1837, stated here as a gap

stops.name: Paris, arrival at about sixteen
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both Wikipedia editions; month and day unknown and defaulted to 01-01. His age on arrival follows from the disputed departure age.
stops.campa: He comes into Paris in the second year of the walk, about sixteen. Louis-Philippe is king, the railways are three years old, and the city still moves its luggage by coach: domed trunks with rounded lids built to shed rain off the roof of a diligence, one trunk on top of nothing. Packing is a trade with its own guild word, layetier-emballeur-malletier, box-maker and packer and trunk-maker in a single title. The boy from the mill puts himself in front of that trade at the moment the railways begin to change what luggage has to survive.
suggested_refs: The trade term layetier-emballeur-malletier, and the domed coach trunk it existed to make

stops.name: Rue Saint-Honore, the workshop of Monsieur Marechal
stops.date_confidence: the apprenticeship is attested; the address is not. '327 rue Saint-Honore' appears only in brand repetition and in no Wikipedia article in either language, so the coordinate is an estimate on the correct street, moved east from the first pass's 48.8676/2.3220 because numbering rises westward. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He is taken on as apprentice to a Monsieur Marechal, an established Paris layetier-emballeur, and stays seventeen years. The work is not the making of trunks alone. It is packing: going into the houses of the rich and folding crinolines and porcelain and hats into cases so that nothing arrives broken. He learns which objects survive a journey and which do not. That is not carpentry, and it is not learned at a bench. The address given for the workshop, 327 rue Saint-Honore, is repeated everywhere in brand literature and appears in no encyclopedia article that could be fetched.
sources: company heritage materials for the street number, unfetchable
suggested_refs: Paris guild and apprenticeship records for the layetiers-emballeurs, 1830s, unconsulted

stops.name: The Tuileries, packer to the Empress
stops.date_confidence: contradiction carried and one branch shown impossible. fr.wikipedia gives 1852, Encyclopedia.com gave 1853, en.wikipedia gives no year at all. Napoleon III became Emperor 2 December 1852 and Eugenie became Empress on marrying him 30 January 1853, so an appointment to an Empress cannot predate 1853. The Tuileries placement is inferred, not attested: no source puts Vuitton inside the palace. Pin inherited byte-identical from empress_josephine.journey.json.
stops.campa: Napoleon III is emperor from December 1852; Eugenie de Montijo becomes Empress on marrying him on the thirtieth of January. Vuitton, still in Marechal's workshop, is made her personal packer, entrusted with the imperial wardrobe: the crinolines that will not fold, the dresses that have to arrive uncreased at Compiegne and at Biarritz. Josephine was installed in these same Tuileries in 1800, and the office of packing an empress's trousseau is older than either woman. The palace will burn in 1871 and be pulled down in 1883, while he is still alive.
suggested_refs: The vanished Palais des Tuileries, seat of the imperial household from Josephine to Eugenie

stops.name: Creteil, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the day is not recovered and is defaulted to 01. The bride's age of 16, given by en.wikipedia, is corroborated by nothing else consulted and is carried as reconstruction. Her birth year is given loosely as 1836-1838. The coordinate is the town centre; the church is named nowhere.
stops.campa: In April, at thirty-two or thirty-three, he marries Clemence-Emilie Parriaux at Creteil, south-east of Paris on the Marne. The English article gives her age as sixteen; nothing else consulted corroborates it, and the church of the ceremony is not named anywhere. She will keep the books of the house he is about to open, follow him out of the city to the workshop by the river, and die ten years before he does. Her year of birth is given only as somewhere between 1836 and 1838, and no register was opened to settle it.
sources: secondary genealogical accounts, exact URLs not captured
suggested_refs: The civil marriage register of Creteil, April 1854, unconsulted

stops.name: 4 rue Neuve-des-Capucines, the sign goes up
stops.date_confidence: the year 1854 and the address are attested by both editions; the month is reconstructed from the sequence, since the marriage is April and the accounts place the founding shortly after. The street is today the rue des Capucines.
stops.campa: Within weeks of the marriage he leaves Marechal after seventeen years and opens his own workshop at number 4 rue Neuve-des-Capucines, one street from the Place Vendome, today the rue des Capucines. The sign advertises fragile objects securely packed and the packing of fashions. He is thirty-two and has the household of an empress on his books. The name over the door will still be over doors a hundred and seventy years later. Nothing in the shop is yet called a monogram, and nothing in it is yet worth forging.
suggested_refs: The shop sign of 1854 advertising the packing of fragile objects and of fashions

stops.name: Paris, the birth of Georges
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the date comes from company heritage materials whose page could not be fetched, and no register was consulted. A contradiction is carried, not resolved: one heritage source calls Georges the only son of the marriage, a separate secondary account describes five children.
stops.campa: Georges Ferreol Vuitton is born in Paris in July. He is the son who will take the house after his father, register the Monogram, and be credited by some sources with the trunk lock that other sources credit to his father. The heritage materials call him the only son of the marriage; a separate secondary account gives the couple five children. Neither claim could be checked against a register in this pass, and the birth date itself comes from house materials whose page returned nothing when fetched.
sources: company heritage materials, exact URL not captured
suggested_refs: Paris birth registers for July 1857, unconsulted; the Wikipedia article on Georges Vuitton returns 404 in both editions

stops.name: Rue Neuve-des-Capucines, the Trianon canvas
stops.date_confidence: attested but on a single source. The 1858 date is en.wikipedia's alone; fr.wikipedia names the toile Trianon grise as a material and gives no year for it. The first pass presented this the other way round. Encyclopedia.com framed it as a development running 1854-1859. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The trunk lid goes flat. Vuitton covers a rectangular poplar frame in grey Trianon canvas, glued and light and airtight, and abandons the domed leather lid that had been built for centuries to shed water off a coach roof. A flat lid can be stacked, and stacking is what a steamship hold and a railway van require. The date is 1858 in the English article; the French article, leaned on here for the Jura and the death, gives no date for the Trianon canvas at all, so the year rests on one source and is marked as doing so.
suggested_refs: A surviving grey Trianon canvas trunk of the late 1850s, flat-topped and stackable

stops.name: Wigmore Street, London, the house of H.J. Cave
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and not a journey: no source consulted puts Vuitton in London at this date, and en.wikipedia's own article on H. J. Cave and Sons makes no mention of him, so the influence rests on a single English article talking about a firm that does not talk back. Cave was founded 1839 and at Wigmore Street from 1856; the first pass's Mayfair coordinate is corrected north to Wigmore Street.
stops.campa: The London firm of H.J. Cave and Sons, founded in 1839 and at Wigmore Street since 1856, is named by the English article as an influence on the flat lid. No source consulted puts Vuitton himself in London in this decade, and the Cave article makes no mention of him; the influence is trade example, not travel. Cave's own shop at 40 Wigmore Street carried a billing that the Vuitton building on the Champs-Elysees will take for itself in 1913, fifty-five years later and across a strait.
stops.quote: the largest travel goods store in the world
stops.quote_source: Billing of H.J. Cave and Sons at 40 Wigmore Street, London, cited in the verification pass; the identical phrase is later applied to the 1913 Louis Vuitton building on the Champs-Elysees
suggested_refs: H.J. Cave and Sons at 40 Wigmore Street, and the phrase two firms used about themselves

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the workshop on the river
stops.date_confidence: contradiction carried, not resolved: fr.wikipedia 'Louis Vuitton' gives 1859, fr.wikipedia 'Asnieres-sur-Seine' gives '1860 - Louis Vuitton installe ses ateliers a Asnieres', en.wikipedia gives no year. The '20 workers' figure of the first pass appears in no reachable source and is dropped. The coordinate approximates the present rue Louis-Vuitton site; the commune centroid is 48.9108/2.2889.
stops.campa: The Paris workshop is too small. He buys land at Asnieres-sur-Seine, downstream and outside the city, where poplar can come in by water and finished trunks go out the same way, and builds an atelier there. The French article on Vuitton dates the move to 1859; the French article on the commune dates it to 1860; the English article gives no year, and no choice is made between them here. The figure of twenty workers, carried by the first research pass, appears in no source that could be reached and is dropped rather than repeated.
suggested_refs: The rue Louis-Vuitton at Asnieres-sur-Seine, named for the workshop that stood on it

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the house against the workshop wall
stops.date_confidence: the family residence beside the atelier is attested in general terms; no source gives a build year, so the date follows the workshop and is defaulted to 01-01. The later renaming of the street and the conversion into the Musee Louis Vuitton come from company materials, not from fr.wikipedia 'Asnieres-sur-Seine', which mentions neither.
stops.campa: He builds the family house against the wall of his own workshop, so that residence and atelier share one plot. Clemence-Emilie, Georges, and the apprentices are all inside the same enclosure, and the poplar comes off the river a few steps from the kitchen. The street will one day be renamed rue Louis-Vuitton and the house will become the Musee Louis Vuitton, though neither detail is in the French article on the commune; both come from company materials. He is thirty-nine and has moved his whole life out of Paris to be next to the water.
sources: company heritage materials, exact URLs not captured
suggested_refs: The founder's house at Asnieres, workshop on one side and family on the other, later the Musee Louis Vuitton

stops.name: Champ de Mars, the Exposition Universelle
stops.date_confidence: attested, and a gap the first pass had declared open is closed: en.wikipedia states that the company participated in the 1867 Universal Exhibition in Paris. What medal, if any, was awarded is recorded nowhere reachable. The fair opened 1 April 1867; the pin is inherited byte-identical from gustave_eiffel.journey.json.
stops.campa: The house exhibits at the Exposition Universelle on the Champ de Mars. The English article states the participation plainly, closing a gap an earlier research pass had left open; what medal, if any, was awarded is recorded nowhere reachable. On this same ground Gustave Eiffel is at work in the Galerie des Machines, twenty-two years before he raises his tower over it. The fair puts the workshop in front of a foreign trade for the first time on record; who bought there, and what they paid, is not recorded either.
suggested_refs: The prize lists of the Exposition Universelle of 1867, unconsulted, which would settle the medal question

segments.name: The War, the Rue Scribe, and the Forgers

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the war of 1870
stops.date_confidence: stated as a gap. No source consulted records what became of the workshop, the stock, or the family during the Franco-Prussian War and the siege of Paris. The first pass's speculation that the suburb sheltered the business is dropped: Asnieres lies outside the fortifications in the zone the Prussian armies occupied. Date defaulted to the opening year of the war.
stops.campa: The war with Prussia and the siege of Paris fall across these two years. Asnieres lies outside the fortifications to the north-west, inside the zone the Prussian armies occupy and fight over, not in the sheltered suburb the house tradition suggests. What happened to the workshop, the stock, and the family in those months is recorded in no source consulted. The gap is stated as a gap: it is not known whether Vuitton lost his atelier in the winter of 1870 or kept it working through the siege.
sources: no source found for the workshop in 1870-71
suggested_refs: The occupied north-western suburbs of Paris, winter 1870-71, and the silence of the Vuitton record about them

stops.name: 1 rue Scribe, the shop by the unfinished opera
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and weakly held. The boutique appears in no article fetchable in either language; fr.wikipedia has no 'Hotel Scribe' article at all (404). The first pass tagged it attested while conceding it could cite nothing. The detail 'beside the newly built Palais Garnier' is wrong for 1871: the opera was unfinished, work halted by war and Commune, and opened only 5 January 1875. The street coordinate is correct.
stops.campa: A shop is said to open at number 1 rue Scribe, beside an opera house that is not finished. The Palais Garnier will not open until January 1875, the work halted first by the war and then by the Commune, so the address in 1871 faces a building site. Surviving trunk locks are said to carry this street stamped into the brass. The boutique appears in no article that could be fetched in either language, and rests only on secondary accounts of the building that later became the Hotel Scribe.
stops.quote: chez Vuitton, le magasin de malles de la rue Scribe
stops.quote_source: French literary text surfaced by a Wikisource full-text search snippet titled 'Mademoiselle Carriere, de l'Odeon'; the document page returned 404 on direct fetch, the passage was never read in situ, and author, edition, and date are unconfirmed
sources: secondary accounts of the rue Scribe address, exact URLs not captured
suggested_refs: Trunk locks of the 1870s stamped with the rue Scribe address, cited but never seen in this research

stops.name: Paris, the trunk that goes to Japan
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year by en.wikipedia's company account; month and day are unknown and the month is set to place the stop after the rue Scribe entry in travel order. Whether Oyama Iwao himself or someone in his circle placed the order is not stated.
stops.campa: A trunk goes to a customer associated with Oyama Iwao, the Satsuma officer who will become field marshal and war minister of Meiji Japan. It is the earliest recorded reach of the house into a country that had been closed to European trade within Vuitton's own lifetime, and it is recorded as a purchase rather than as a journey: the order is placed in Paris and the trunk travels by sea. What was in it, and whether Oyama or someone in his circle bought it, the English company article does not say.
suggested_refs: Oyama Iwao, and the first recorded passage of a Paris trunk to Meiji Japan

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the striped canvas
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year by both en.wikipedia and the Encyclopedia.com entry the first pass used; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The grey Trianon canvas is being copied. Vuitton replaces it with a beige and brown striped canvas, made at Asnieres, chosen because a stripe is harder to counterfeit than a plain weave. It is the first of three pattern changes forced on the house by forgers; the stripe, the checkerboard, and the monogram are all made against copying before any of them is an ornament. Within a decade the imitators have copied the stripe as well, and he will have to change the cloth again.
suggested_refs: The beige-and-brown striped canvas of 1876, the first pattern invented against forgers

stops.name: Boulevard Malesherbes, the clientele of a quarter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and an inferred overlap rather than a documented meeting. No source names Vuitton in Proust or Proust in Vuitton. The pin is inherited byte-identical from marcel_proust.journey.json, where it marks the family flat of 1880.
stops.campa: On the boulevard Malesherbes a nine-year-old asthmatic named Marcel Proust is living in his parents' flat, in the quarter whose salons order their travelling cases from the rue Neuve-des-Capucines. The clientele Proust will spend thirty years describing, the Guermantes side and the Verdurin side, is the clientele Vuitton has been packing for since the Second Empire. No source names Vuitton in Proust or Proust in Vuitton. The overlap here is an address book and a set of staircases, nothing more, and is marked as such.
suggested_refs: The salons of the eighth arrondissement in 1880, customers of one trade and subject of another

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the death of Clemence-Emilie
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the year comes from a secondary genealogical account and no source consulted gives the place, the day, or the cause. Asnieres is used because it is where the family lived in that decade, not because any document says so.
stops.campa: Clemence-Emilie Parriaux dies. The year comes from a secondary genealogical account; no source consulted gives the place, the day, or the cause, and Asnieres stands here because it is where the family lived by this decade and not because any document says so. She had been married to him twenty-eight years and had watched the house go from a rented shopfront near the Place Vendome to a riverside atelier with a street of its own. Louis Vuitton will outlive her by ten years and will be buried in the same town.
sources: secondary genealogical account, year only, exact URL not captured
suggested_refs: The death record of Clemence-Emilie Parriaux, 1882, place unknown, unconsulted

stops.name: Oxford Street, London, the first store outside France
stops.date_confidence: attested and doubly sourced, retagged upward from the first pass. en.wikipedia: opened its first store in London on Oxford Street. fr.wikipedia: 'En 1885, une premiere boutique ouvre hors de France, avec succes, sur Oxford Street a Londres.' The shopfront number was not recovered and the coordinate is a generic point on the street.
stops.campa: The house opens a store on Oxford Street, the first outside France, and both the English and the French articles say so. London is where the flat lid had been anticipated by H.J. Cave a quarter of a century earlier; the Paris firm now sells into that market on its own account. Whether Louis Vuitton crossed the Channel for the opening is not stated in any source consulted. He is sixty-four and the house is thirty-one years old. The counterfeiters follow it across the water within a few seasons.
suggested_refs: The Oxford Street shopfront of 1885, number unrecovered, first Vuitton address outside France

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the checkerboard and the words in the weave
stops.date_confidence: the Damier of 1888 is attested by both editions; the exact quoted string is carried as reconstruction, since no primary image or period trademark filing could be fetched to confirm it in situ. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The checkerboard. Brown and beige squares, and printed into the pattern the words that make the cloth itself a legal document: the mark is registered, and copying it is theft of a trademark rather than imitation of a design. The pattern is put on the canvas because a court can read it. The Damier is the last of the three canvases Louis Vuitton introduces himself. The third and most famous, the Monogram, will be drawn by his son four years after the funeral, out of his father's initials.
stops.quote_source: Trademark text woven into the Damier canvas of 1888, reproduced across company histories and museum catalogue notes; no primary image or period filing could be fetched, so the exact string is unverified
suggested_refs: A Damier trunk of 1888 with the registration formula printed into the weave

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the lock that cannot be picked
stops.date_confidence: contradiction carried, not resolved. en.wikipedia's designer material credits the pick-resistant lock to Louis; Encyclopedia.com credited the five-tumbler patent to Georges in 1890. The sources are not consistent on who patented which lock and when, and this atlas does not adjudicate. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: A lock that cannot be picked, with one key opening all of a single customer's cases, becomes part of the house's claim on the trade. The English article credits Louis with it; the American encyclopedia credits the five-tumbler patent to Georges in 1890. The two accounts are not reconciled anywhere reachable and are not reconciled here. What the lock changes is the object it closes. The trunk has stopped being furniture that travels and become a strongbox that travels.
suggested_refs: The French patent file for the five-tumbler trunk lock, which would settle the attribution, unconsulted

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the explorer trunks
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout: the series is described by secondary accounts whose exact URLs were not captured, dated only to the 1890s, and the personal involvement of Louis Vuitton rather than of the workshop generally is not established in any source consulted. Date set at the start of the decade.
stops.campa: Zinc, copper, and brass are hammered over poplar at Asnieres for trunks meant to survive tropical damp, ordered by travellers bound for Africa and Asia; Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza is named among the customers. The series runs through the 1890s, which is to say it begins at the very end of Louis Vuitton's life and continues for years under his son. Whether the founder himself worked on the explorer trunks is established in no source consulted, and the whole item rests on secondary accounts alone.
sources: secondary historical accounts of the explorer-trunk series, exact URLs not captured
suggested_refs: The metal-clad explorer trunks of the 1890s, and the question of whose hands built them

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the death of Louis Vuitton
stops.date_confidence: attested; day, month, year and place given by both Wikipedia editions.
stops.campa: He dies on the twenty-seventh of February at Asnieres-sur-Seine, seventy years old, in the house he built against his own workshop wall. Fifty-seven years earlier he had walked out of a mill in the Jura with no trade and no money and two years of road in front of him. He leaves a firm with a London store, an atelier on the river, three canvas patterns invented to defeat forgers, and a son of thirty-four who has been at the bench since boyhood. The monogram that will carry his initials around the world does not yet exist.
suggested_refs: The house beside the atelier at Asnieres, where the founder died in February 1892

stops.name: Cimetiere de la rue du Menil, the burial
stops.date_confidence: the cemetery is attested by two independent sources, closing a gap the first pass had declared unresolvable: Wikidata Q277616 gives the Cimetiere ancien d'Asnieres-sur-Seine, and fr.wikipedia 'Asnieres-sur-Seine' states he is buried 'au cimetiere de la rue du Menil'. The date of the funeral is not recorded and is defaulted; the coordinate approximates the town, since the cemetery's own point was not recovered.
stops.campa: He is buried in the old cemetery of Asnieres-sur-Seine, on the rue du Menil, a few streets from the workshop. Wikidata and the French article on the commune both name the ground, which closes a gap an earlier research pass had declared unresolvable. What remains unknown is narrower and stranger. Whether the grave of the man whose name is now on shopfronts in every capital carries any monument, inscription, or stone at all is described in no source consulted. That, and not the cemetery, is the gap.
suggested_refs: The old cemetery of the rue du Menil at Asnieres-sur-Seine, and an unphotographed grave

segments.name: The Monogram, Which He Never Saw

stops.name: Paris, Georges draws the Monogram
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year by both editions; month and day unknown and defaulted. All sources consulted agree that Louis Vuitton did not design it and that it postdates his death by four years.
stops.campa: Georges draws the Monogram: his dead father's initials interlocked, with quatrefoils and four-petalled flowers taken from the Japanese design then fashionable in Paris, and patents the pattern worldwide. It is made, like the stripe and the checkerboard before it, to be hard to copy. So the pattern begins as a defence against copying, and it carries the initials of a miller's son who never saw it drawn. Every source consulted agrees that Louis had no hand in it.
suggested_refs: The 1896 Monogram canvas, a dead man's initials patented against forgers

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the trunks cross the Atlantic
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the pin and date are inherited byte-identical from victoria_ocampo.journey.json for her first crossing to Paris, and no source ties Ocampo luggage to the Vuitton workshop. The link asserted here is the route and the trade, not a receipt.
stops.campa: Victoria Ocampo crosses to Paris for the first time, sixteen years old, one of the Argentine families that shuttle between Buenos Aires and the Right Bank with steamer trunks in the hold. The trans-Atlantic traffic the house built after 1854 runs on exactly this kind of passage: the flat lid exists because a ship's hold stacks. Buenos Aires is weeks from Le Havre. No source ties the Ocampo luggage to the Asnieres workshop, and the connection recorded here is the route rather than a receipt.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires to Le Havre steamer route, and the stackable trunk it was designed for

stops.name: Champs-Elysees, the largest travel goods store in the world
stops.date_confidence: the 1913 opening and the billing are attested by en.wikipedia; month and day unknown, defaulted. The coordinate is corrected from the first pass's 48.8698/2.3079, which was Wikipedia's centroid for the whole avenue; the store stands at no. 101 near the Etoile end.
stops.campa: The Louis Vuitton Building opens on the Champs-Elysees, at the Etoile end of the avenue, and is billed as the largest travel goods store in the world, which is the phrase the London firm of H.J. Cave had used of its own shop in the decade the flat lid was invented. Twenty-one years after the founder's death the house has a monument on the grandest avenue in Paris, and the trunk trade has become an address. The war that will empty the avenue of its customers is a year away.
suggested_refs: The Louis Vuitton Building of 1913 on the Champs-Elysees, and the borrowed superlative on its front

stops.name: Paris, Gaston-Louis and twenty-five models a year
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on a single secondary chronology, now unreachable. Georges's tenure to about 1936 and Gaston-Louis's from 1936 to 1970 rest on Encyclopedia.com alone, whose page 301-redirects to 404. The Wikipedia articles for Georges Vuitton and Gaston-Louis Vuitton return 404 in both editions, re-confirmed in the verification pass.
stops.campa: Gaston-Louis Vuitton, grandson of the founder, takes the house and holds it thirty-four years. Between 1959 and 1965 the firm is credited with launching some twenty-five new luggage models a year, a figure that comes from one secondary chronology and is carried here as reconstruction rather than fact. Georges's own tenure, from 1892 to about 1936, rests on the same single source. The Wikipedia articles for both Georges and Gaston-Louis Vuitton return 404 in English and in French alike.

stops.name: 10 avenue George V, Balenciaga opens a house
stops.date_confidence: attested for Balenciaga, inherited byte-identical from cristobal_balenciaga.journey.json. The relation to Vuitton is geographic and anachronistic with respect to the founder: it is placed in the posthumous segment for that reason.
stops.campa: Cristobal Balenciaga opens his house at number 10 avenue George V, a few hundred metres from where the Vuitton flagships will later stand. The quarter that Louis Vuitton entered in 1854 as a trunk maker with an imperial client has become, by this decade, the address of the entire French luxury trade. Balenciaga is leaving a war in Spain; Vuitton had walked into this city from a mill in the Jura. The two arrivals are a century apart and end on the same six streets.
suggested_refs: The avenue George V and avenue Montaigne corridor, address of a trade that began with packing cases

stops.name: Hotel du Parc, Vichy, the shop on the ground floor
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and held on one relay. fr.wikipedia 'Louis Vuitton Malletier' dates the period 'de 1940 a 1944' and is the source of the year; month and day are defaults and carry no claim. The boutique itself is given no date by anything reached. The Hotel du Parc claim comes from Dirk de Klein, 'Fashion and Fascism', dirkdeklein.net, 24 September 2025, crediting Vogue UK and The Guardian of 3 June 2004; theguardian.com and web.archive.org are both blocked to this session's fetch tool, so neither named original was read. The French article names the Hotel du Parc nowhere.
stops.campa: The government of the French State installs itself in a spa town and takes the Hotel du Parc for its offices. On the ground floor of that building there are shops. The jewellers Van Cleef and Arpels are shut down; the trunk maker is not, and is the only one permitted to stay open under the Marshal's windows. This rests on one blog of 2025 relaying Vogue and the Guardian, and on no page that could be opened in this pass. The name over the door is the name of a boy who walked out of the Jura in 1835 with nothing.
stops.quote: Louis Vuitton had a store on the ground floor of a fabulous property, the Hotel du Parc in Vichy, where Petain set up his puppet government
stops.quote_source: Dirk de Klein, 'Fashion and Fascism', dirkdeklein.net, 24 September 2025, read in situ; the page credits Vogue UK and Kim Willsher's Guardian article of 3 June 2004, neither of which could be fetched in this pass, so this is a relay and not a primary reading

stops.name: Paris, the busts of Marshal Petain
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact, undated as to the year, and unlocated. en.wikipedia's raw wikitext, read in situ and cited there to Kim Willsher, The Guardian, 3 June 2004, gives 'more than 2,500 busts' glorifying Petain; fr.wikipedia 'Louis Vuitton Malletier', citing Bonvicini 2004, gives the loyalty and the objects but neither the number nor a place. No source consulted says where they were made, so the generic Paris pin used elsewhere in this file for unlocated corporate facts is used again and Asnieres is deliberately not pinned. The date is set inside 1940-1944 and is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The house affirms its loyalty to the regime of Marshal Petain and agrees to manufacture objects to his glory: more than two thousand five hundred busts, by the English article citing a Guardian investigation that could not be opened here. Where they are cast is named in no source consulted. Gaston-Louis, grandson of the founder, is said to have instructed his eldest son Henry to forge links with the regime. Henry is decorated, by Nazi Germany in the French account and by the Nazi-backed government in the English. No choice is made between them here.

stops.name: 30 avenue Montaigne, Dior opens a house
stops.date_confidence: attested for Dior, inherited byte-identical from christian_dior.journey.json. The later common ownership of these addresses and the Vuitton name is a twentieth-century corporate fact and carries no implication about the nineteenth-century house.
stops.campa: Christian Dior opens at thirty avenue Montaigne, one street over, the year after the occupation ends. The Corolle line will be shown in these rooms in February, and the trunks that carry it abroad are still made of poplar and canvas. Within four decades the corporate structure that owns the Vuitton name will own this address too. Nothing in 1946 predicts that: Dior is a dealer's son with backing from a textile fortune, Vuitton is a family trunk firm with an atelier by the Seine, and what links them is a postcode.
suggested_refs: Thirty avenue Montaigne, 1946, one street from the corridor Vuitton's successors would occupy

stops.name: Paris, Barthes reads the fashion press
stops.date_confidence: attested for Barthes; the pin is inherited byte-identical from cristobal_balenciaga.journey.json, where the same stop appears. The juxtaposition with Vuitton's canvases is this atlas's own and is not claimed as a source relation.
stops.campa: Roland Barthes publishes the Systeme de la mode, having read the fashion press rather than looked at the clothes, and finds that what the trade sells is a system of signs. Vuitton had reached a working version of the same conclusion in 1876 and again in 1888, by a shorter road: he changed his canvas twice because the pattern, and not the box, was the thing being stolen. The forger and the semiologist agree about what a monogram is for. Neither of them mentions the other.
suggested_refs: Systeme de la mode, 1967, and three canvases invented eighty years earlier for the same reason

stops.name: Paris, Moet Hennessy and four letters
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia 'LVMH'; month and day unknown, defaulted. Moet Hennessy was itself formed in 1971 from Moet & Chandon, established 1743, and Hennessy, founded 1765.
stops.campa: Louis Vuitton merges with Moet Hennessy, itself assembled in 1971 out of a champagne house of 1743 and a cognac house of 1765, and the initials LVMH are made from three family names, two of them older than the third by a century. The trunk firm founded by a walker from the Jura is now a letter and a half in an acronym. In October the stock market crashes across the world, and the shareholders of the newly merged company begin looking for someone with money.
suggested_refs: The 1987 merger deed, and the three surnames compressed into four letters

stops.name: Paris, Arnault takes the chair
stops.date_confidence: contradiction carried, not resolved. en.wikipedia 'LVMH' has Arnault chairman and chief executive since January 1989; fr.wikipedia 'LVMH' has him taking some 40 per cent with Guinness after the October 1987 crash and becoming 'officiellement patron de LVMH en avril 1990'. Both accounts stand; the date here follows the English one and the French one is stated in full.
stops.campa: Henry Racamier, running the Vuitton side, invites Bernard Arnault in as an investor against his own partners. Arnault takes some forty per cent with Guinness after the crash and does not leave. The English account has him chairman and chief executive from January 1989; the French account has him officially installed as patron in April 1990. Both are carried and neither is adjudicated. The house passes out of the founder's family altogether and into the hands of a man who bought it.
stops.quote: Si en sortant du casino il n'avait pas eu ce furieux besoin d'argent, s'il n'avait pas vu soudain toutes ces liasses bourrant le grand sac Vuitton, si la femme etait sortie dix minutes plus tot ou plus tard, si...

An anti-prison polemic, not fiction: the bag is a passing prop in a hypothetical robbery, a vessel for stolen banknotes, and the text is of 2004 and can support no claim about the nineteenth-century house

stops.name: Bois de Boulogne, the Fondation opens
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected. Both en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia give 20 October 2014, not the 27 October the first research pass carried from memory. Gehry, the Bois de Boulogne, the address 8 avenue du Mahatma-Gandhi, and the presence of President Francois Hollande are all confirmed; the coordinate matches Wikipedia's exactly.
stops.campa: Frank Gehry's glass sails open in the Bois de Boulogne on the twentieth of October, inaugurated with the President of the Republic present, and the founder's name is fixed to a museum of contemporary art at 8 avenue du Mahatma-Gandhi. Louis Vuitton made boxes for other people's possessions, glued and airtight and opaque. The building that carries his name is a box for paintings, glazed so that the box itself can be seen through. He has been dead a hundred and twenty-two years and the mill at Anchay is a ruin.

stops.name: Asnieres-sur-Seine, the bench still working
stops.date_confidence: attested in the present tense by fr.wikipedia, which gives roughly 180 artisans at the Asnieres atelier; the date is a placeholder for an ongoing condition and is defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The workshop at Asnieres is still working, some hundred and eighty artisans making bespoke and special-order trunks on the ground he bought for the river, and the family house beside it is a museum. The house presents this as an unbroken line back to the founder's own bench, which is what a house is for. Of the man himself the documents give a birth at a mill, a walk of two years, a marriage, three canvases, a workshop, and a grave on the rue du Menil with nothing recorded on the stone.
suggested_refs: The Asnieres atelier and the Musee Louis Vuitton, a working shop and its own archive
